newsitem.title: UK: Call for rate rise is premature-UK business chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Call for rate rise is premature-UK business chiefs.

text.p: The Bank of England's call for higher interest rates just a week after the last rate rise is premature, British business chiefs said on Tuesday.
But they still backed the new Labour government's decision to grant the central bank independence.

Delegates gathered for the British Chambers of Commerce's annual conference in the Welsh capital said they were concerned at the Bank's tone in the inflation report and suggested it should have waited for the budget, expected in early June.

"This call for higher rates unnerves me," said David Owen, a sales manager for Hofland Deltflex, a manufacturer of industrial gaskets. "This is very early to be calling for a rate rise when so many factors are unknown, like the contents of the budget."

His company is heavily dependent on overseas markets and he was concerned to hear the pound had jumped more than a pfennig after the Bank of England's inflation report. "This is not good for companies like us. The pound's strength is very damaging."
The BCC represents thousands of small businessmen across Britain. Few would disagree with Owen.
"I'm a bit concerned at this news. It is a very fast response after only a week," said Mark Donegan, a consultant for Cardiff Bay Concepts, a marketing consultancy.
Last Tuesday, the Bank was granted operational control over interest rates and Chancellor of the Exchequer also agreed to the bank's call for a quarter point rate rise.
Earlier on Tuesday, the Bank said in its quarterly inflation report that is unlikely that underlying inflation will be below the government's target of 2.5 percent in two years' time.
"On the present evidence, there is still likely to be a need for some further moderate tightening of policy in the months ahead," it said.

But while the BCC delegates were wary of the Bank's fresh assault on inflation, many welcomed its new powers and praised the new government for taking such a bold decision early in the administration.
Labour's first policy decisions were shrewd and showed an impressive amount of forward planning, they said.

"Giving the Bank control over interest rates was a very shrewd move. It is very welcome for business to take the direction of monetary policy away from political influence," said Tony Burkitt, a management consultant to manufacturing firms in Lincolnshire.
"The pace at which the government is moving is very impressive. It has planned very well for government," said John Forkin, strategic director at the South Derbyshire Chamber of Commerce.
But business people said they were anxious that the growing economy inherited by the Labour government should not be held back due to worries about overheating.
The recovery has so far combined steady growth with low inflation, but some commentators have said the robust growth in consumer demand and spending is a cause for concern.

"The windfall payments from building societies is posing a problem, but there is a danger that (the authorities) will do too much to offset it," said Peter Rhodes of Peter Rhodes Ltd, an electrical goods retailing group in Lincolnshire.
"This government has been handed a steadily growing economy and should tread very carefully when it comes to restraining demand."
A total of more than 20 billion pounds in shares will be paid to members of building societies which are converting into banks this year.

Business leaders were also wary of the planned windfall tax on privatised utilities. "It is retrospective, so a little unfair, and the uncertainty over the level of the tax is damaging," said Burkitt.
But he welcomed the government's early budget. It has not yet confirmed the date for the budget, but there is speculation it will be on June 10.
